Candidate sampling changes metric values and sometimes model rankings; popularity sampling does not automatically reproduce full-catalog evaluation. [Sequential-recommendation experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13045) and [candidate-set sampling research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11723) support treating uniform, popularity-matched, TF-IDF-neighbor and model-mined panels as different evaluation conditions. A defensible paired design—an inference from this evidence—uses identical user/history/target rows, fixed panel sizes, unique candidates, identical seen-item exclusions and deterministic sampling. Define common-row eligibility before scoring: every retained row must support all four constructions. Report eligibility counts and exclusion reasons by category; separately report broader coverage so complete-case results are not generalized to excluded users.

For missing metadata, distinguish absent text, empty TF-IDF vectors and insufficient eligible neighbors; report their frequencies. Use a shared text-eligible candidate universe for the controlled comparison, with explicitly labeled fallback analyses separately. Measure pairwise candidate overlap/Jaccard and realized panel sizes; retain natural overlap in the primary comparison, since forcing disjointness changes the constructions. Compute popularity from training interactions only; match or stratify candidate popularity and report target-popularity and history-length strata. These are proposed controls, motivated by evidence that [candidate selection interacts with popularity bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11723), rather than an established four-panel protocol.

Freeze TF-IDF fitting and mining models using permitted training data; never select candidates using held-out labels. Preserve benchmark splits while auditing information available at prediction time, since [temporal leakage can change model rankings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060). Pair comparisons within history, aggregate repeated prefixes within user, and bootstrap users rather than treating overlapping histories or repeated candidate draws as independent observations. Reuse the same trained category model across panels; report paired effects and uncertainty.
